title: Shame and Motivation Don't Mix
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart Jr. argues that poor student motivation should never be met with shame, even when a teacher is bluntly correct that grade-mongering represents genuine motivational poverty. Drawing from a passage in The Will to Learn, he distinguishes between students who perform school tasks and students who genuinely care about learning — contending that high-achieving but grade-obsessed students are, by a meaningful definition, poorly motivated, but that this condition is not their fault and must not be treated with contempt. He makes the crucial observation that students want to want to learn — that the preference for genuine motivation over apathy is inherent — meaning the teacher's role is to tend the soil in which genuine care can grow rather than to shame students out of shallow motivation. The postscript delivers the article's most direct claim: shame feels like a tool because it occasionally produces compliance, but it is actually a slow-working poison that decays the soul.
points: Distinguish between students who perform school tasks well and students who genuinely care about what they are doing; high academic achievement does not guarantee authentic motivation.

Grade-obsessed or accolade-seeking students are, in Stuart Jr.'s framework, poorly motivated — but this is not a moral failing, and teachers who respond with judgment or contempt are compounding the problem.

Students universally want to want to learn; the preference for genuine motivation over apathy is already present in every student, meaning the teacher's job is to restore access to that native desire rather than manufacture it from scratch.
The teacher's practical role is environmental: tend the soil, water, weed — partner with the power already in the seed, which requires treating every student as a human being brimming with dignity.

Shame is not merely ineffective as a motivational tool; Stuart Jr. argues it is actively deceptive and harmful — appearing occasionally to work while actually functioning as a slow-working poison that erodes the soul.
quotes: A person who does a thing — who even does it well — is not necessarily a person who cares about what they've done. Instead, the person can be driven by care for the carrots or the sticks. This, in my observation, is the condition of most folks who do well in our secondary schools today.

What I'd like to put forth in this book is that such a person, regardless of grades or achievement, is actually a poorly motivated human soul. They'll do work, but it won't be done from the fullness of their agency. And so, eventually, they'll find themselves alienated from the fundamental goodness of learning. They'll lose the sensory capacity for tasting and seeing that an education is good.
What I'm writing about today is the reality that being poorly motivated isn't something anyone should be ashamed of. And we should never cast aspersion on a student who is poorly motivated in school.
Students want to want to learn. They'd much prefer the state of motivation to the state of apathy. We are all alike in this preference.
The thing to do is treat them like a human being brimming with dignity and do the kinds of things that can help the seeds of true care grow. You can tend the soil. You can water and weed.
Shame is a terrible and counterproductive tool. It is also a deceitful tool — it seems like it works sometimes, but what it actually does is poisons the soul.
